items.why: The quoted sword command targets followers, but the woman’s ensuing execution makes the competitor reasonably ambiguous.
The passage explicitly names Abishai’s victim and clearly distinguishes him from David.
The man of God explicitly intercedes after the king asks for prayer.
Elisha’s direct reply to the officer’s doubt is clearly separated from his earlier price prophecy.
Their decision to report immediately follows their admission that hiding the news is wrong.
Narrative order identifies Sibbekai as the first killer, though “who kills first” is slightly artificial.
The refusal is explicitly grounded in the Lord’s command, not the offer’s size.
The three aided conflicts are explicitly listed and contrasted with the tribute-paying Ammonites.
The negative wording is somewhat stiff, but the unchanged evil ways are stated directly.
Uzziah is clearly the person whom Azariah and the other priests follow.
The people take Uzziah and make him king, though the purpose phrasing is mildly awkward.
The letter heading cleanly distinguishes its writer, Claudius Lysias, from its recipient.
The speaker explicitly says that her own son was cooked and eaten first.
The prophet brings the body to his city before placing it in his tomb.
Talking until daylight is the event immediately preceding Paul’s departure.
The two centurions clearly receive the order, while the soldiers form the detachment.
Entering the city follows the proposed capture, but the question awkwardly treats the king’s speculation as fact.
The returning group is recoverable from the contrast with the cavalry, though “soldiers” can also include cavalry.
Evil spirits explicitly leave, but “on the items’ arrival” is an unnatural and only implied formulation.
The off-duty companies receive the specific temple-guarding assignment, despite the passage’s complex syntax.
The final clause identifies Uzziah as the soil lover, but the question is unusually phrased.
The summary attributes all four defeats to David and his men, while Jonathan kills only the described individual.
Both the commander’s consent and Paul’s resulting transfer could reasonably be prerequisites for the ambush.
Paul’s intention to leave the next day is explicitly given as the reason for his prolonged speech.
The quoted plan clearly assigns the other woman’s child to tomorrow.
Jeroboam’s command unambiguously refers to the man of God.
The messengers’ return and report occur directly before the people plunder the camp.
Elisha calls the person sending the messenger a murderer, clearly indicating the king.
The passage explicitly says Uzziah was eager to leave because the Lord afflicted him.
The action sequence clearly begins with Ben-Hadad mobilizing his army.
Zechariah is explicitly identified as Uzziah’s instructor in the fear of God.
The practitioners burn the scrolls immediately after bringing them together.
The trampled victim is explicitly the officer assigned to the gate.
The warning is addressed directly to the man of God from Judah, not the old prophet.
The writer explicitly orders the man’s accusers to present their case to the recipient.
Jehoiada gives the weapons, while David is identified only as their former owner.
Athaliah goes to the people because she hears the noise; seeing the king happens afterward.
The passage directly attributes the city’s calm to Athaliah’s death.
The 307,500 soldiers are explicitly placed under the command of the 2,600 family leaders.
The old prophet mounts the donkey after his sons saddle it for him.
“The news” merely repeats the question and does not state what information was reported.
The beaten group who flee naked and bleeding is clearly the seven sons of Sceva.
The Arameans identify the hired Hittite and Egyptian kings as the expected attackers.
The narrative antecedent identifies the traveling man of God as the lion’s victim.
The officer is explicitly trampled, fulfilling the man of God’s warning.
Paul directly says that the young man has something to tell the commander.
Within the old prophet’s claimed message, the man of God is the one invited to eat and drink.
Jotham’s succession is the event stated after Uzziah’s burial.
The prophecy explicitly assigns the priests’ sacrifice to the future son named Josiah.
The conspirators ask the council to petition the commander to bring Paul.
The intended messenger is recoverable, but repeated pronouns make the question confusing about who declares and who predicts.
Joash is explicitly hidden with his nurse at the temple for six years.
The men clearly decide to go to the Aramean camp and surrender rather than enter the city.
The first covenant explicitly joins the Lord, the king, and the people, unlike the second covenant.
